doc.title: Steve Buckingham, interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, February 25, 2019 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Barry Beckett, Richard Tee and the King Curtis band behind Aretha
summary: Discussing Barry Beckett's number-chart playing on Paul Simon's record and the King Curtis band behind Aretha in 1969.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: I remember getting fooled on a Paul Simon record. I said, that’s got to be Richard T. And it wasn’t. It was the guy from Muscle Shoals.

Barry was a dear friend of mine. He died ten years ago or so. But yeah, I know Richard T and I know all those players. Cornell Dupree was one of my idols in New York on guitar — “Rainy Night in Georgia” and all that stuff. But Richard T was obviously magnificent as were a lot of guys. But Barry Beckett was as good as anybody. Paul Simon’s “Still Crazy After All These Years” where it’s just Barry on the Fender-Rhodes, and Paul Simon. And Barry told me that Paul made him do it in every key. I mean every key: A, B flat, B, C, C sharp. He had to play it in every — and if you listen to “Still Crazy After All These Years” it’s not an easy chord progression, just the — Barry wrote his numbers out. That’s the great thing about a number chart. You can write the numbers out and then okay I’ll play it in A. Now let’s do it in B flat. I still read the same numbers I just go up a half a step. That was the great thing about a number chart. So he played all those versions of “Still Crazy” for Paul Simon from a number chart. And when it was over Paul Simon picked the take and when he listened to it, it’s a classic. And like I say he could play as good as anybody. Richard T or any of those guys. And I saw all the great ones. When I first saw Aretha in ’69 it was the King Curtis band. Cornell Dupree, Jerry Jemmott on bass, Billy Preston on organ, and Richard T on electric piano and a great horn — the drummer was Bernard Purdie, Pretty Purdie.

No. And besides the New York horn section they brought in the Memphis horns. Two white guys and a black guy from Memphis to play. It was an unbelievable band. They opened the show and then Aretha comes on. And that’s the same thing when you see Aretha live, the record “Aretha Live at the Filmore West” when Ray Charles came. That was that band. Yeah. Billy Preston playing organ for God’s sakes. I mean, but I saw all those guys play. And Tom Scott did one in New York called the New York Connection with Pretty Purdie and all those guys. He’d hang up a sign when he was playing a session, whatever it was, his 15,101 session. He’d have a little sign he’d hang up every — there’d be a different sign.
